newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Concordsky Tu-144 flies again.
newsitem.headline: Russian Concordsky Tu-144 flies again.

text.p: Russia's 1970s supersonic Tupolev-144LL "Concordsky" jet, rescued from the aviation scrapyard to perform tests for U.S. manufacturers, took to the skies on Friday at a military air base near Moscow.
The drop-nosed and delta-wing aircraft was airborne for 40 minutes, the first of 32 experimental flights which the Tupolev company plans to make during the next six months.

Alexander Pukhov, Tupolev's chief designer, told a news conference that the Tu-144LL jet, fitted with updated electronics and upgraded engines, would help Russia and the United States to develop the technology for a high-speed civil transport for the next century.
"It will be a supersonic jet with capacity of carrying 300 passengers with a speed of 2,400 km per hour (1,500 mph). The jet may begin flights in 2006," he said.
Pukhov said the world's airlines would need about 500 such jets in the next century.
Tupolev will conduct the Tu-144LL test flights using money from a group of U.S. aviation companies udner a programme run by NASA, the U.S. space agency.

Tupolev's U.S. partners under the project -- Boeing Co, McDonnell Douglas, Rockwell, United Technologies' Pratt and Whitney unit and General Electric -- were putting $10 million into the first stage of the project. Pukhov said the Russian side's contribution was around one-third of this.
Pukhov also said the test results would be used by Tupolev company and its U.S. partners.

"We hope to take part in development of the new supersonic jet offering our jet wing developments and some other technologies, if we prove our capabilities," he said, adding that Tupolev did not have enough money to develop a second-generation supersonic jet on its own.

Sergei Borisov, Tupolev's chief test pilot, said after the first Tu-144LL's return to the sky that it was a very important flight. "We are restoring the supersonic programme to reach a new era of world civil aviation," he told Reuters.
The jet flew at an altitude of 2,000 metres (6,600 ft) at a speed of 450 km per hour (280 mph) in low cloud.
Pukhov said that his first impression from the flight was positive. "I am waiting for the crew's comments on it," he said.
But the Tu-144LL's debut was disturbed by several dozen women workers from the Tupolev company who held a protest meeting before the flight to demand payment of 18 months unpaid wages.
Tupolev's general director Valentin Klimov said the company had serious financial problems last year. "We hope such international projects will help us to get out of deep crisis," he said.
The original Tu-144 aircraft made its first flight on December 31, 1968, just days before the Franco-British Concorde, earning the Soviet rival the nickname "Concordsky" in the West.
Aeroflot, the Soviet carrier, used some Tu-144s, which could carry up to 160 passengers at 2,400 km/h (1,490 mph), on its route from Moscow to the Kazakh capital Almaty.
But the development programme was quietly shelved after a crash at the 1973 Paris Air Show which killed 13 people.
At present, the only commercial supersonic airliners flying are the few Concordes still operated by British Airways and Air France. Their slightly slower top speed is 2,179 km/h (1,354 mph).
The last test flight by the one remaining Tu-144 took place six years ago.
